tldr: This paper uncovers a surprising fact: vision-language models (VLMs) used to evaluate videos tend to prefer aggressive, jerky gaits. To address this, the authors propose PhySA, which decouples visual aesthetics and physical smoothness into two independent reward channels to achieve smooth humanoid locomotion.
hero_caption: Overview of PhySA and main findings: left shows the smoothness comparison against Prompt2Policy; middle depicts the reward framework separating visual aesthetics (VLM) from physical corrections (simulator state); right highlights the 24x reduction in API calls and ablation results.
overview:
When deploying humanoid robots in the real world, achieving smooth motions that minimize sudden joint acceleration and jerk is critical. Reinforcement learning (RL) without explicit smoothness penalties often produces jerky, high-energy gaits that swing joints aggressively. Recently, using vision-language models (VLMs) as reward sources has gained attention: by feeding rollout videos to a VLM, it returns an aesthetic quality score on a 0 to 10 scale without requiring tedious task-specific feature engineering.

However, across four production VLMs (including GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet, and Gemini Pro), the authors discovered a startling contradiction: VLMs assign higher aesthetic scores to gaits with larger joint acceleration, perceiving them as more confident and active (mean Pearson correlation $r = +0.66$). Using a VLM score directly as a proxy for physical smoothness actually encourages the robot to learn violent, jerky movements.

To resolve this conflict, the authors introduce PhySA (Physical Smoothness and Aesthetics), a reward framework that cleanly decouples visual aesthetics and physical smoothness into separate channels. A sparse, asynchronous VLM channel handles coarse posture and symmetry evaluation, while an adaptive physical correction module monitors simulator states and adjusts joint acceleration penalties across training phases.

Evaluated on MuJoCo Humanoid-v5, PhySA reduced joint acceleration by 59.5% and mechanical power by 43.1% compared to Prompt2Policy in a single extended run. However, the authors candidly report that a three-seed replication yielded a smaller, non-significant reduction of 7.2%, and the performance gain failed to transfer to other simulators (IsaacLab) or robot models (Unitree G1) due to differences in numerical integration schemes.
contributions: Quantitatively demonstrated that aesthetic scores from production VLMs correlate positively with joint acceleration (mean $r = +0.66$), failing as a proxy for physical smoothness.

Proposed PhySA, a reward framework that pairs an asynchronous, low-frequency VLM evaluation channel with a phase-triggered physical correction channel that adjusts penalty weights based on training statistics.
Reduced VLM API calls by a factor of 24 compared to synchronous baselines (costing roughly $0.85 per 10M steps) without blocking the training loop.
Investigated the failure of smoothness reward transfer across simulators (MuJoCo to IsaacLab), identifying physical engine sub-step numerical integration differences as the primary cause.

sections.heading: Why shouldn't you trust a VLM's eye for 'natural' motion?
sections.summary: Smooth joint trajectories are essential for real-world humanoid deployment. Ironically, when VLMs rate locomotion videos, they award higher scores to jerky, aggressive gaits. This paper dissects this conflict and proposes PhySA to separate aesthetic and physical rewards.
sections.details:
To operate humanoid robots stably in the real world, policies must generate smooth trajectories that limit actuator wear, conserve energy, and remain trackable by low-level motor controllers. However, standard RL optimizing primarily for forward progress inevitably yields high joint acceleration $\|\ddot{\mathbf{q}}\|_{2}$ and erratic motion.

Tuning a fixed smoothness penalty coefficient is notoriously tricky. If the penalty is too high early on, the robot destabilizes and falls; if it is too low, jerk remains unchecked. To bypass hand-crafted feature engineering, recent approaches like Prompt2Policy rely on pre-trained VLMs to evaluate gait aesthetics directly from rendered videos.

Yet this approach carries a major pitfall. Testing across four commercial VLMs revealed that gaits with higher joint acceleration consistently received higher aesthetic ratings (mean Pearson $r = +0.66$). VLMs tend to interpret large, swinging limb motions as confident strides, while judging smooth, conservative gaits as stiff.

Directly substituting VLM aesthetic scores for smoothness rewards pushes the policy in the wrong direction—toward rougher motions. To fix this, PhySA separates aesthetic rewards (from the VLM) and physical smoothness rewards (from simulator state variables) into two completely independent, non-interfering channels.

sections.heading: Current landscape: VLM rewards, code synthesis, and smoothness regularization
sections.summary: Existing methods suffer from the heavy cost of per-step VLM queries and fixed reward weights that cannot handle mid-training shifts. PhySA solves these issues via asynchronous queries and dynamic, phase-based reward adjustments.
sections.details:
Prior work broadly falls into four categories:

### Policy Learning with Vision-Language Models (VLMs)
Frameworks like LIV and RoboCLIP compute dense rewards from joint video-text embedding spaces, but ignore physical smoothness. Synchronous methods like Prompt2Policy query GPT-4 class models at every policy update, blocking the training loop and burning through over 1,200 expensive API calls per 10M steps. PhySA lowers this to one asynchronous call every 200k steps (50 calls total, a 24x reduction), cutting latency and cost dramatically.

### LLM Code Synthesis for Rewards
Eureka and Text2Reward use LLMs to synthesize reward code from natural language instructions. However, once the best reward function is selected, it remains static throughout training, leaving it unable to fix emergent reward hacking or unwanted behaviors. PhySA monitors training statistics at phase boundaries to modify penalty weights dynamically.

### Smoothness Regularization in Humanoid RL
Techniques such as action rate penalties, gradient surgery, and imitation-based motion priors set their reference trajectories or weights before training begins. A static penalty introduced too early can derail learning, while introducing it too late cannot undo established jerkiness.

### Evaluation Biases in VLMs
While LLM generation biases (such as verbosity bias) are widely studied, quantitative verification in robotics has been scarce. This paper is the first to show that commercial VLMs exhibit a consistent bias toward aggressive, high-acceleration motions.

sections.heading: Inside PhySA: Decoupling aesthetics and physics into dual channels
sections.summary: PhySA decomposes the per-step reward into four terms: task reward, VLM aesthetic channel, physical correction channel, and a Gaussian motion prior. The VLM evaluates overall posture asynchronously every 200k steps, while the physical correction module tunes specific joint penalties at 2.5M step intervals upon detecting plateaus.
sections.details:
The core design of PhySA is a clean separation of concerns. Posture aesthetics and symmetry—observable from a single video frame—are delegated to the VLM. In contrast, time derivatives such as joint acceleration—which cannot be resolved from static frames—are computed directly from simulator state variables.

The overall step reward $r_{\text{total}}$ is defined as:
$$r_{\text{total}} = r_{\text{task}} + \alpha\,r_{\text{VLM}} + r_{\text{phys}} + r_{\text{GMP}}$$
where $r_{\text{task}}$ is the base forward locomotion task reward, $r_{\text{VLM}}$ is the aesthetic channel, $r_{\text{phys}}$ is the physical correction channel, and $r_{\text{GMP}}$ is a Gaussian motion prior fitted to motion capture data to keep poses within a natural envelope.

### 3.1 Task Reward
To maintain a fair comparison with the Prompt2Policy baseline, this term remains untouched. It consists of a 0.5 m/s velocity tracking term, a survival bonus for keeping torso height, a height penalty, and actuator energy costs.

### 3.2 Aesthetic Reward Channel (VLM Channel)
Every 200k steps, a background thread renders a 12-frame video clip (0.4 seconds) and sends it to GPT-4o. The prompt asks the model to evaluate knee usage, left-right symmetry, and center-of-mass tracking, returning an overall score on a 0 to 10 scale. This score is smoothed using an exponential moving average (EMA) and injected as a per-step reward $r_{\text{VLM}} \in [-0.5, +0.5]$, with its weight fixed at $\alpha = 0.5$.

Crucially, because this reward remains constant over each 200k-step window regardless of the immediate state or action, it does not guide instantaneous joint angles. Instead, it effectively scales the survival bonus, rewarding the policy for staying alive longer with an aesthetically pleasing posture.

### 3.3 Physical Correction Channel
The 10M-step training budget is split into four 2.5M-step phases. At each phase boundary, the system checks recent logs across posture stability, energy efficiency, and episode return. Only if progress plateaus or stability degrades does the trigger fire, raising actuator penalties on high-velocity joints or pruning unhelpful penalties. In two primary experiment runs, adjustments were triggered at 3 out of 8 phase boundaries (37.5%).

captions.F2: End-to-end architecture of PhySA. The top aesthetic channel asynchronously queries GPT-4o in the background and applies EMA smoothing, while the bottom physical correction module detects plateaus at phase boundaries (every 2.5M steps) to dynamically update physical penalty weights.

sections.heading: Experiments: What drives smoothness, and why did cross-simulator transfer fail?
sections.summary: In MuJoCo, PhySA cut joint acceleration by 59.5% and mechanical power by 43.1% in a single run. Ablations confirmed that the physical correction channel drove the smoothness gains. However, transferring the policy to IsaacLab failed due to differences in integration time steps.
sections.details:
The experiments addressed three core questions: RQ1 (Can smoothness coexist with walking performance?), RQ2 (Which module drives smoothness?), and RQ3 (Does the gain transfer to other simulators or robot platforms?).

### 4.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations used Stable-Baselines3 PPO on MuJoCo Humanoid-v5, treating Prompt2Policy as the primary baseline. Smoothness is measured by the joint acceleration norm $\|\ddot{\mathbf{q}}\|_{2}$.

### 4.2 Smoothness Gains and Energy Conservation (RQ1)
In a single extended run, PhySA reduced joint acceleration by 59.5%, lowered mechanical power per step by 43.1%, and increased episode length by 57% relative to Prompt2Policy (though a three-seed replication yielded a non-significant 7.2% reduction).

The energy-saving mechanism is particularly intriguing: 95.3% of the total power reduction came from just two joints: sagittal pitch and yaw in the hips. While the overall torque norm increased slightly (+6%), the joint velocity norm dropped sharply by -35%. PhySA did not simply relax the whole body; it achieved smoothness through joint specialization—isolating motion to a few joints and moving them slowly.

### 4.3 Component Ablation (RQ2)
Evaluating each channel in isolation highlighted their direct opposition:
- VLM aesthetic channel only: Roughness (acceleration) surged by +136% (resulting in violent movements, but earning the highest VLM score).
- Physical correction module only: Roughness dropped by -29.8% (though VLM scores declined).

This confirms that the physical correction channel is entirely responsible for the smoothness gains.

### 4.4 Sim-to-Sim Transfer Failure and Diagnostics (RQ3)
Directly porting PhySA to IsaacLab with the same task and model produced only an insignificant -1.0% to -2.2% change in smoothness. Rescaling penalty coefficients by 50x to 60x did not help.

Investigating the root cause within MuJoCo by changing the integration step $\Delta t$ from the default 0.015 s (with 5 sub-steps) to 1/60 s caused joint acceleration to worsen nearly fivefold. The presence of fine sub-step integration to smooth contact spikes proved decisive for the acceleration penalty's effectiveness. Experiments on a Unitree G1 model similarly yielded no significant gains, exposing a strong dependency on simulator integration schemes.

captions.F4: Ablation results across reward channels. Running the VLM channel alone (purple) increases roughness by 136%, while running the physical module alone (orange) lowers roughness at the expense of aesthetics. Only PhySA (green star), which combines both, reaches the Pareto frontier.
captions.F5: Cross-simulator transfer evaluations. While MuJoCo shows substantial roughness reduction (green), transferring to IsaacLab (both direct transfer and 50–60x rescaling) as well as push-recovery tests fall within the noise floor (gray).

sections.heading: Takeaways and future challenges
sections.summary: Because VLM aesthetic scores favor violent movements, they cannot act as proxies for physical smoothness. PhySA addresses this by separating the two channels, but challenges remain around seed variability and sensitivity to numerical integration schemes.
sections.details:
The primary takeaway of this study is clear: never substitute VLM aesthetic evaluations for physical control qualities like smoothness. Evaluating video clips holistically leaves VLMs blind to high-frequency acceleration, leading them to reward exaggerated motions. PhySA acknowledges this fundamental trade-off and decouples the reward channels, achieving marked jerk reduction and power savings in MuJoCo.

Nevertheless, the authors candidly highlight several key limitations:
- The maximum improvement (-59.5%) came from a single run; a three-seed replication yielded a non-significant -7.2%, reflecting high variance across random seeds.
- Because the current VLM reward is a static scalar over 200k steps, it functions primarily as a survival bonus multiplier rather than providing fine-grained, state-conditioned guidance.
- The method is highly sensitive to the physics engine's numerical integration scheme, preventing zero-shot transfer to IsaacLab or real-world morphologies like the Unitree G1.

Despite these caveats, the paper offers valuable cautionary insights for anyone looking to incorporate multimodal foundation models into robotic reward design.

sections.heading: Appendix: Power breakdowns, ablations, and baseline comparisons
sections.summary: Detailed joint power breakdowns, reward hacking tests (bait rewards), and comparisons with Eureka and Vanilla PPO. The analysis reveals that power savings concentrate heavily in the legs, and exposes how Eureka falls prey to reward hacking by vibrating in place.
sections.details:
### Joint-by-Joint Power Breakdown (B.1)
Leg power consumption plummeted by -73.7% (-486 W), while torso and arm power increased by +25.9% (+80 W). Remarkably, right hip pitch and left hip yaw accounted for 95.3% of the total net power reduction (406.6 W). As the legs moved more slowly, the arms and torso compensated to balance angular momentum.

### Reward Hacking Experiments (Appendix E)
To test whether VLMs dislike smoothness or simply get misled by flashiness, the authors designed a 'bait' reward that kept upper-body posture clean while intentionally making lower-body joints jerk violently. The VLM awarded this bait policy roughly the same score (4.8 to 5.0) as PhySA, proving that VLMs focus on overall visual appeal and fail to penalize severe lower-body jerk.

### Pareto Comparison with Other Methods (B.4)
At 2.6M steps, PhySA lowered joint acceleration by -25.7% vs. Vanilla PPO, -26.6% vs. Text2Reward, and -31.7% vs. Eureka. Notably, rewards auto-generated by Eureka triggered reward hacking: the robot vibrated in place to collect survival bonuses without walking forward. PhySA's phase monitoring detected and corrected such stagnation within a single phase.

captions.F6: Power consumption breakdown by joint group. Power in the legs dropped by 73.7%, with two hip joints accounting for 95.3% of total net power savings.
captions.F7: Pareto frontier of smoothness versus episode length at 2.6M steps. Eureka suffers from reward hacking by vibrating in place without moving forward (red cross), whereas PhySA (green star) minimizes acceleration (693), securing the smoothness frontier.

takeaways: VLMs exhibit a strong aesthetic bias toward high-energy, dynamic movements; never use their scores directly as rewards for joint smoothness or energy efficiency.
Visual aesthetics (observable from still frames) and physical smoothness (evaluated via time derivatives) must be designed as completely independent, decoupled reward channels.

Smoothness penalties are exceptionally sensitive to the physics engine's internal integration time step and sub-step count. Transferring rewards across simulators requires matching numerical integration resolution, not just tuning weights.
limitations: The dramatic joint acceleration reduction (-59.5%) was observed in a single run; a three-seed replication yielded a smaller, non-significant reduction of -7.2%, indicating high variance across seeds.
Because the VLM reward is a fixed scalar updated only every 200k steps, it cannot intervene in specific poses or gait phases, acting primarily as a scaled survival bonus.
Smoothness improvements failed to reproduce when transferred to IsaacLab or the Unitree G1 model, showing limited robustness across different simulators and robot morphologies.
